title: When Beaver Fur Was Money: What Could You Buy?
alternate_titles: How Much Could a Beaver Pelt Buy in 1733?
Shopping When Your Money Was Fur
period: Fort Albany trading post, James Bay, 1733. An illustrative visit built around the 1733 Standard of Trade printed by Arthur Dobbs in 1744, pp.193–196. Northern woodland and low riverbank; restrained timber trading-room reconstruction, not a claimed measured plan. Summer visit with stored pelts; separately labelled winter labour and European hat-making explanation. Indigenous trading parties are knowledgeable customers, not a generic Plains-western cast. European clerks wear plain early-eighteenth-century shirts, waistcoats and breeches. Indigenous adults wear restrained practical hide and traded-cloth garments; no invented ceremonial regalia or uniform costume. Exact everyday garment silhouettes require the visual-reference gate. Visitor retains the approved modern orange hoodie as a quiet observer.
avoid: No Canadian dollar prices, maple-leaf flags, decimal currency, metal made-beaver tokens, four-stripe modern HBC point blankets, shopping carts, Victorian shop signs, industrial factory chimneys, York boats, cowboy hats, Plains feather warbonnets, teepee village used as a generic national stereotype, mountains on James Bay, modern muskets or firearms, gun-height stacks of pelts, blood or trapping demonstrations. No live beaver exchanged over the counter. Do not treat every skin as one unit regardless of quality. No 'all Indigenous people' claims. Do not import York Factory prices or New York's Fort Albany buildings. No generated writing, numerals or price labels.

counter.design: Plain plank counter with window on left, cloth shelves on rear right, broadcloth bolt on low rack, brass cooking kettle with bail handle on right shelf, closed fur bundles below counter. Restrained early-eighteenth-century timber interior; no exact floor-plan claim. Fix these landmarks. Two adult Indigenous customers and one European clerk, all equal adult scale and composed expressions.

river.scope: Fort Albany region, James Bay, summer 1733
river.design: Low wooded riverbank and shallow landing, birchbark canoe drawn alongside with cargo secured inside. Spruce and birch in low flat terrain. Small undetailed timber store behind trees. No landmark fort silhouette invented; no mountains, steamer or later York boat.

goods.scope: Analytical close-ups of goods listed in the 1733 tariff
goods.design: Neutral parchment and one plain timber surface. Depict a single good or matched pair clearly, without accidental quantities. Exact counted sets and all prices are local graphics, never model-painted numbers.

winter.scope: Explanatory winter labour in the James Bay hinterland, early eighteenth century
winter.design: Snowy spruce and birch woodland with adult travellers carrying a closed bundle, practical winter layers. No hunting method, animal injury, precise route or named historical family invented.

hatter.scope: Explanatory European beaver-felt hat-making context, early eighteenth century; not Fort Albany
hatter.design: Small European workshop with low plain benches, dark unfinished felt hat bodies and simple wooden hat blocks. No industrial machinery, top hats of a later fashion, tail sewn onto hat or stuffed-beaver hats.

cloth.design: Same restrained counter geometry as main room; macro views of a plain broadcloth bolt, edge, weave and hands assessing fabric. Any bale-seal explanatory close-up is a separately labelled museum-derived diagram, not an assertion of a specific seal's discovery on this counter.

gifts1706.scope: Documented Albany trading-party gift account, 1706; explicitly a flashback
gifts1706.design: Low river landing and simple timber doorway. Trading-party leader meets European trader at equal height. Coat and small wrapped goods exchanged with measured respectful gestures. Do not invent ceremonial pipe ritual or exact appearance of Whatting; no staged quote.

ledger.scope: Modern explanatory graphic; source is Dobbs 1744 describing 1733
ledger.design: Locally composed source excerpts, comparisons and basket arithmetic on channel parchment. Clear headings; six unit counters are abstract squares, not historical coins. Scope and source remain visible.

sources.title: Arthur Dobbs, An Account of the Countries adjoining to Hudson's Bay (1744), Standard of Trade, pp.193–197
sources.read: Original OCR pp.193–197 read; pp.193–194 inspected in the browser at readable enlargement on 2026-10-09. A second 1744 scan (cihm_35075) cross-checked. Printed 1733 date, blanket six, pound-based brass-kettle rate, breeches three, hooks twenty and knives eight confirmed visually.

Do not adopt his moral judgments, geographical claims or 'fair price' assumptions. The OCR misreads 1733 as1753. Modern summaries and the UVic transcription contain material numeric errors.

chapters.title: Your money has fur
scenes: Twenty fishhooks. That is one option. A blanket is another—but the blanket will swallow six times as much of your budget.
One simple iron fishhook on timber; room for local quantity and price card.
You have arrived with fur, and you would like to leave with things your household can actually use.
Two adult trading visitors unload a closed dry fur bundle from a birchbark canoe; no animal carcass.
Before you agree to anything, there are three questions. What counts as money, what can it buy, and who gets to decide?
Three-question opening card, one question revealed per cut.
WHAT COUNTS? / WHAT CAN IT BUY? / WHO DECIDES?
Welcome to Fort Albany on James Bay, in seventeen thirty-three. We are following an imagined visit using a real trade list.
Reframe river landing with low timber store partly behind trees; Visitor on unobstructed near bank.
The list measures value in beaver skins. The accounting term you will hear is made beaver: the value of a prime pelt.
One abstract unit square beside a folded fur illustration; clearly explanatory.
MADE BEAVER / A UNIT OF VALUE
That matters. A bundle of ten skins does not automatically mean ten identical units, regardless of the skins inside it.
Establish room: left window, right shelves and kettle, counter with closed bundles; customers and clerk facing each other.
You can also bring other furs. They are valued against the beaver standard, which gives different goods a common measuring stick.
Two differently sized closed fur parcels beside clerk's blank ledger; avoid identifying unsupported animal skins.
Think of the unit as the language of the deal. The actual things changing hands still have to be examined.
Customer and clerk both assess folded fur on counter with calm attentive faces.
And the blanket hanging behind the counter is already making our little shopping problem harder. Six units for one item.
Plain unstriped folded wool blanket, distinct from later HBC point blankets.
Why does the fur have that much purchasing power? The answer takes us a long way from this trading room.
Look past fur bundle toward open doorway and river light; preserve counter landmarks.
Somebody on the other side of the Atlantic wants a hat. Your household wants useful goods. This trade connects those wishes.
Folded fur at left and dark felt hat silhouette at right; no whole animal hat.
But getting from a beaver to a shopping budget involves rather more work than walking up to a counter.
Canoe cargo at low landing, adults lift a compact bundle carefully; no extravagant treasure chest.

chapters.title: The work inside the bundle
scenes: For Cree traders in this region, the journey to bayside posts could be made in birchbark canoes.
Close birchbark canoe side with ribs and secured cargo; one wooden paddle; no later cargo boat.
The fur trade fitted around seasonal work. Families also needed food, shelter and the resources to keep going through the year.
Adults sort modest travel bundles beside canoe; no invented numbered household ration.
Winter was an important season for acquiring the pelts that traders wanted. We are briefly stepping back from the summer landing.
Winter woodland explanatory anchor with two fully clothed adults walking with closed bundle; no trapping action.
Now our tidy unit of value contains weather, travel and labour. The price list does not tell us how many hours each pelt required.
Snow-dusted footwear and bundle carried above snow; stable adult anatomy.
Across the ocean, the sought-after material is the beaver's soft underfur. That is the part especially useful for making felt.
Simple locally drawn fur cross-section distinguishes long guard hairs and soft underfur; no microscopic realism claim.
Canadian Museum of History · Fur trade
We should picture a hat-maker working with felt, rather than someone attaching a complete furry skin to a hat.
European workshop anchor with dark felt hat bodies, plain wooden blocks, craftsperson at bench.
The finished object can look very different from what left James Bay. The material has changed form along the way.
Dark smooth felt hat body on wooden block; no beaver tail or ears.
That distant demand helps explain why a bundle on this counter can be exchanged for cloth, metal goods or sugar.
Fur parcel foreground, folded cloth and kettle in established rear shelf, no lettering.
It does not mean everyone in the chain wants the same thing. A trader bringing fur is also a customer choosing imported goods.
Indigenous customer gestures toward cloth while clerk waits; equal height and agency.
The surviving list comes to us in Arthur Dobbs's book, published eleven years after the year it describes.
Locally typeset date pair with source title shortened; no generated book text.
It lets us test specific prices. It does not preserve our imaginary visitor's receipt, or every conversation that could change a deal.
Blank ledger page and customer's hand resting beside goods; no fake documentary signature.
So let us begin with something small enough to overlook. On this list, one unit can buy twenty fishhooks.
One iron fishhook enlarged for clarity; exact quantity will be shown in next chapter's local graphic.

chapters.title: Small goods, real choices
scenes: Twenty fishhooks for one beaver unit. Put them beside eight knives, which the same list also values at one unit.
Local two-row price comparison;20hooks in4rows5 and8knives in2rows4, accurate distinct objects.
Those are alternatives. Handing over one unit does not buy both piles, however enthusiastically our Visitor points at them.
Two separated neutral display trays with representative hook and knife; local price labels and OR, not counted generated piles.
A small object can have a very practical job. These are choices about equipment, rather than a cupboard full of curiosities.
Iron hook and plain utility knife on timber, handle and blade safely at rest.
Now try clothing. One pair of breeches costs three units in the printed schedule. Knee-length trousers take a larger bite.
Plain early-eighteenth-century knee-length breeches laid flat, no modern jeans or full-length trousers.
The blanket costs six. You cannot infer the price just from whether an object looks large or small on the shelf.
Folded unstriped blanket beside representative small tool, prices absent until local overlay.
The arithmetic is straightforward. The decision is personal: warmth, clothing, tools, or something else your household needs.
Customer considers shelves without comic confusion; Visitor remains secondary at frame right.
Our list also offers sugar: two pounds for one unit. A shopping decision can include wants as well as essential equipment.
Unwrapped pale sugar pieces on plain balance pan; no branded bag or modern measuring label.
There is no universal basket everyone must take home. A standard unit makes the alternatives comparable; it does not choose them for you.
Customer places selected plain cloth beside bundle while leaving other goods on shelves; illustrative decision.
Even the word 'one' needs attention. One pair, one pound, one yard: those are very different quantities.
Three clean unit labels with trouser, weight and cloth icons.
A yard of broadcloth is listed at two units. A pound of thread is also two. The unit beside the good matters.
Cloth length and thread bundle in separate zones; quantities and prices added locally.
If we flatten that table into 'one object for one beaver', we change the deal before anyone has even agreed to it.
Simplified incorrect one-for-one assumption crossed through, correct weight and length labels retained.
And that mistake becomes especially obvious when we pick up the kettle.
Customer lifts simple brass cooking kettle by bail handle just above counter; grounded wrist and correct gravity.

chapters.title: The kettle trap
scenes: The important word here is pound. The list prices brass kettles at one pound of kettle for one beaver unit.
Exact local price card with kettle icon and weight symbol; not a tea kettle.
That is not a promise that every kettle on the shelf costs one. A heavier one changes the arithmetic.
Two brass cooking kettles with clearly different size, identical construction family; no price painted on them.
For a simple example, a three-pound kettle would work out at three units under that rate. We are calculating, not reading a receipt.
Three unit squares beside locally labelled3lbkettle; label example clearly.
You would also care about the object itself. Its listed weight cannot tell you whether it is the kettle you actually want.
Hands examine rim and bail fittings of brass cooking vessel; no invented defect assumed.
The same caution applies elsewhere. A number helps compare a trade; it does not replace looking closely at the goods.
Customer looks along cloth edge while clerk holds opposite end; no customer passively accepting unwanted item.
The schedule even gives guns a range of ten, eleven or twelve units. There is no instruction here to stack pelts to barrel height.
Local text-only historical rate card with small neutral long-gun silhouette, no handling demonstration.
Powder, shot and flints have their own entries. The equipment in a trade is not captured by one dramatic picture of a gun.
Closed plain powder container, lead-shot pouch and flint shown separately at rest; no loading or ignition.
Put the price list down for a moment. The person on the other side of the counter has standards too.
Indigenous customer's focused expression, cloth in hands; clerk attentive rather than dominant.
Museum research describes customers checking the quality of imported cloth and demanding better stock when it was defective.
Establish macro cloth view tied to counter geometry; customer examines weave near window.
Canadian Museum of History · Sealed and Delivered
That is a very different scene from someone accepting anything shiny. The choice concerns what the goods are like in use.
Fingers test cloth edge and drape, restrained texture rather than sparkles or treasure.
A common measuring unit can make a discussion easier. It cannot force a dissatisfied customer to like the fabric.
Customer sets one cloth bolt aside and looks to another; reconstruction, no staged angry confrontation.
And cloth leaves a surprisingly small clue behind in the archaeological record.
Tiny dull lead seal beside folded cloth on neutral surface, diagrammatic form without invented readable mark.

chapters.title: The customer inspects the goods
scenes: Cloth itself can decay. The small lead seals attached to bales are much more visible to archaeologists studying the trade.
Schematic cloth-bale seal enlarged beside soft fabric silhouette, labelled as explanatory.
Canadian Museum of History · bale seals
A seal could record a standard of length, weave or colour, or show that a tax had been paid.
Three cloth-standard icons and separate tax-record icon; no promise that every seal certifies all four.
It was not a little beaver coin. A small metal disc in a trading story can have an entirely different job.
Lead seal attached by short strip to cloth wrapping, not loose spending token; no currency symbol.
English seals have been found at Fort Albany. The museum also compares seals from French trading posts farther south.
Simple locally drawn site list; no unverified exact map route or French seal attributed to Albany.
Fort Albany / Fort Frontenac / Fort Michilimackinac
Those finds help reveal an appetite for imported textiles, including different weights and colours—not simply whatever cloth happened to arrive.
Several restrained cloth rolls in brown, muted red and blue; customers compare two, not a modern fabric shop.
The museum describes traders looking for suppliers who could satisfy that demand before competitors did.
Clerk compares stock with customer's chosen sample; blank ledger on counter, no invented written order.
So the shopper with fur is helping shape what crosses the ocean in the other direction.
Secured cloth bundle loaded into same canoe at landing; fur parcel remains back at post, illustrative exchange.
We can see both sides now. European buyers value beaver fur. Indigenous consumers assess the goods offered in return.
Two-way arrow between labelled fur and imported goods, equal visual weight; no universal win-win badge.
That does not tell us every bargain was fair. It does tell us to take the customers' judgment seriously.
Customer pauses over proposed goods, clerk waits; avoid smiles implying universal satisfaction.
Nor should we assume the price stays the same when we move to a different post.
The same kettle and blanket remain in frame while local comparison card prepares to enter.
The note above this very list warns us about that. It compares Albany and Moose with York and Churchill.
Four locally typeset place names in two groups, tied to a short source-note paraphrase.
The difference, in Dobbs's explanation, is competition.
Wide low river landscape with distant branching water, no false same-day rival shop next door.

chapters.title: A price is not a law of nature
scenes: Dobbs says the standard at York and Churchill is higher, because French traders are not as close to challenge the Company there.
Attributed source paraphrase compares nearby competition; no invented numeric York price.
LESS NEARBY COMPETITION / HIGHER LISTED TERMS
Around Albany and Moose, he says French competition interferes more with the Company's trade. His price list arrives with an argument attached.
Illustrative canoe on a river bend with secured goods; no French fort invented within view.
That helps explain why we have stayed with one place and year. Another post's numbers would make a different shopping basket.
Fort Albany1733scope stamp remains, other undated locations fade; no real price converted.
It does not mean every customer can casually walk down the road to a rival shop. Distance and relationships still matter.
Long low river reach and canoe near shore, enough space conveys travel without unsupported route distance.
The post sits inside a much wider world of journeys, households and trading parties. Our counter scene shows only one part.
Several adults prepare travel bundles together, no exact population or all-male monopoly asserted.
In an earlier account from Albany, seventeen oh-six, a leader named Whatting arrived with twenty canoes.
Distinct 1706 flashback: representative canoe landing. Show the number twenty in a local label; do not generate an exact fleet.
He received a coat, tobacco, knives and a hatchet. This was a gift to a trading-party leader, not our universal shopping allowance.
Coat and wrapped goods offered to an adult leader. No portrait claim, ceremonial costume or generated exact quantities.
The example shows why a list of prices cannot capture every exchange that mattered around the post.
Coat passes between hands while other party members wait; restrained respectful gesture.
Leadership and personal relationships belonged in the story alongside bundles and arithmetic. We now return to our seventeen thirty-three example.
Return to the original 1733 room and fictional customer identities. Do not reuse the 1706 leader as a named 1733 customer.
There is another complication. Sometimes goods could be advanced before the furs that would repay them arrived.
Blank ledger beside an equipment parcel, clerk's hand poised to record; explanatory scene without a forged credit contract.
That changes the question from 'what can I take home today?' to 'what will this relationship require later?'
Customer looks from goods to ledger, composed serious expression.
Fur as money does not make the future disappear.
Canoe at landing points toward the river journey; no invented debt prison or coercion scene.

chapters.title: The goods before the furs
scenes: Historian Richard Preston places the beginning of equipment credit at Moose and Albany sometime between seventeen twenty-six and seventeen thirty-seven.
Local date interval with 1733 inside the range; do not label a single invention year.
Supplies could be given on the expectation of later fur returns. The arrangement connected more than a single visit.
Equipment bundle on counter; adjacent space for a later fur return is empty. No modern loan form.
We should not turn that into a modern payment plan, complete with invented instalments. The evidence describes its own relationships and obligations.
Simple goods-now and furs-later sequence. No interest rate, deadline or mandatory term.
Nor does it mean every person here has the same debt. Our price-list exercise cannot supply somebody's missing account.
Two distinct customers beside separate bundles; no identical debt labels.
It does mean a shopper's position could depend on what had already been promised, as well as what was on the counter.
Goods and open blank ledger share the composition; hands paused rather than shaking on an agreement.
And a household could value the same item differently according to what it already owned or needed.
Well-used plain kettle beside a newer one; condition is illustrative, without a documented specific defect.
Our imagined six-unit budget is deliberately simpler. We are using it to understand the list, not impersonate an actual family's accounts.
Six abstract square counters, label illustrative example. No historicalmetalcoins.
We have checked quantities, noticed quality and kept the prices in their setting. Now we can make a choice without changing the rules midway.
Established room with goods separated into two zones; do not show both alternatives as purchased.
The first option is easy to describe: one blanket. The printed price uses all six units.
Single plain wool blanket at left; right clear for six locally drawn unit counters.
The other option starts with the breeches at three. That leaves three units to spend on smaller purchases.
Knee-length breeches folded neatly; running total added locally, not generated.
We can buy the twenty hooks, the eight knives and the two pounds of sugar—one unit for each listed quantity.
Three goods rows combine into a mixed basket, each worth one unit. Render quantities locally.
Add them to the breeches, and the total is six. Two very different ways to use the same budget.
Breeches at three plus three one-unit purchases equals six. Blanket at six on the opposite side, separated by OR.

chapters.title: What would you take home?
scenes: Here is the choice: one blanket, or a pair of breeches, twenty hooks, eight knives and two pounds of sugar.
Final locally drawn basket comparison; match every quantity and price exactly.
ONE BLANKET / OR THE MIXED BASKET
Both use six units in this exercise. That does not tell us which is the better choice for a real household.
Customer looks between two goods zones; no invented historical dialogue.
If warmth is the urgent problem, a collection of small objects may be a poor substitute for the blanket you came for.
Blanket texture close-up with representative small tools farther back; an explicitly hypothetical choice.
If you already have bedding, the mixed basket may look more useful. The price list gives comparisons, not a shopping conscience.
Breeches and representative small goods on wood. Exact counts belong to the local graphic, not the generated background.
And before saying yes, you still need to look at the goods, agree on the value of the furs and understand the terms.
Hands assess cloth and fur from opposite sides; calm negotiation with no forced celebratory handshake.
That is what our strange-looking currency has revealed. This is a conversation about quality, needs and bargaining, as well as numbers.
Whole room: customer choosing cloth, clerk attentive, Visitor secondary at right.
The beaver unit makes different things comparable. It does not make every pelt identical, every post equal, or every transaction fair.
Three short qualifier cards under MADE BEAVER; no universal equality or fairness badge.
So: which basket would you take home? And what would you want to inspect before you handed your fur over?
Open choice: blanket at left, mixed basket at right represented by a few objects and local quantity labels. Visitor gives a quiet shrug.
A list that starts with beaver skins has led us to household decisions we can recognise, even when the money looks unfamiliar.
Folded fur parcel and plain blanket in soft window light; no historical money coin.
Behind the bundle are people's work and journeys. Behind the imported goods are other people's demands, plans and expectations.
Customers return to the same birchbark canoe with a closed goods bundle; do not assert which basket was purchased.
The counter is where those stories meet. What leaves it matters just as much as what arrives.
Counter clear except folded fur and blank ledger; stable landmarks, no fabricated receipt.
And our Visitor has learned to ask one more question before choosing a kettle: how much does it weigh?
Visitor on bank glances toward plain store; canoe and closed bundle behind. Do not generate him carrying a kettle.

research: The episode is a practical shopping puzzle at Fort Albany,1733. Start with twenty hooks versus a blanket, then reveal why 'one beaver' is a unit rather than a simple animal count. Anchor numeric statements to the original Dobbs1744scan; pp.193–194 were visually inspected on2026-10-09. Original lists blanket6,breeches3,8knives/1,20hooks/1,kettle1lb/1,sugar2lb/1,broadcloth1yard/2,thread1lb/2. Modern heritage-derived tables often flatten the right column and misstate blanket/breeches prices; the UVic compilation independently mistranscribes other rows. Reject both for numeric authority. Use two source-based surprises: a kettle's weight changes its price, and Indigenous customers actively assessed imported cloth. Context is specific and relationships unequal; neither naive-barter caricature nor universal golden-age claim. No actual1733shopping receipt, exact household budget, exact fort plan or finished costume reference is claimed. The final six-unit choice is our arithmetic demonstration. Primary text is colonial and argumentative, not neutral access to Indigenous voices; source labels remain clear. Source-image and garment shape gate is separate from these factual checks.
description: At Fort Albany on James Bay in1733, a trade list valued fishhooks, clothing, kettles and sugar in beaver units. But a pelt was not a fixed-price shopping voucher. We follow an imagined visit to explore the real prices, the importance of quality, and the relationships behind the trade. Prices follow the1733schedule printed by Arthur Dobbs in1744; the customer and six-unit shopping example are illustrative.
pinned_comment: With six units in our example, would you choose the blanket or the mixed basket—and what information would you want before agreeing to the trade?

thumbnails.rationale: Concrete surprising quantity verified from the original; unit qualifier prevents physical-pelt oversimplification.

thumbnails.headline: CHOOSE ONE
thumbnails.background: Single plain unstriped folded wool blanket on left; right remains reserved for Visitor. A small local graphic inset will show the alternative basket; no model-painted price labels.
thumbnails.rationale: Invites a decision; exact alternative basket only from the approved arithmetic spec.

shorts.title: When twenty fishhooks cost one beaver unit
shorts.hook: A price that sounds strange until you check the units.
shorts.description: From the1733trade schedule printed by Arthur Dobbs in1744. A made beaver is a unit of value; this is not a universal one-skin price.

shorts.title: The price of a kettle depended on this
shorts.description: The1733list quotes brass kettles by weight. Our three-pound example is arithmetic, not a surviving receipt.

shorts.title: Your six-beaver shopping decision
shorts.hook: One blanket, or this whole mixed basket?
shorts.description: An illustrative comparison using the1733schedule: one blanket or breeches,20hooks,8knives and2lbof sugar. Listed rates do not guarantee a particular historical sale.

wardrobe.reason: Visitor is a modern observer. No invented Indigenous costume, regalia or trader uniform. Keep the orange hoodie visually secondary.
wardrobe.production_review: Same face, skin, hair and proportions; separate approved composited poses. Historical locals need restrained regional clothing references, not national costume shorthand.

entries.note: James Bay post, not the New York city.

pronunciations.rule: Say made beaver clearly as an accounting term. Avoid reading long source titles or unexplained jargon aloud.

sound_plan.music: Quiet channel theme with spacious timber-room ambience; no cinematic frontier or Indigenous-stereotype music.
sound_plan.mix: Narration first. No gunshots, animal distress, cash-register ding or sparkling coin noises.

new_assets.description: Soft small object placed on timber.
